strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: The domestic couple becomes the hardest hire in Europe, and the pay for the job has doubled in a decade
lead.standfirst: Requests for live-in couples across France, Switzerland and Monaco have risen by more than 60 per cent in three years, while the pool of people willing to do the work keeps getting older.
lead.body:
In 2026 a domestic couple working a villa, a château, a chalet or a large private estate in France, Switzerland, Monaco or Belgium is paid from 4,500 to 6,000 euros net a month for the two of them together. That figure sits on top of independent accommodation, generally on the property or immediately beside it, fully equipped and separate from the main house, and in most placements a service vehicle with fuel and maintenance covered. In Switzerland the equivalent package runs from CHF 120,000 to CHF 160,000 gross a year. In Monaco it runs from 80,000 to 115,000 euros gross.

Between 2015 and 2018 the same pairing was hired for from 3,000 to 3,500 euros net, accommodation included. Morgan & Mallet, which has recruited into private households since 2015 and reviewed the market in a January analysis updated in May, states plainly that this lower band has now disappeared from the professional market altogether. The doubling is not a spike. It is the result of demand that has outrun supply for a decade and shows no sign of correcting.

The demand side is measurable. Internal agency data shows an increase of more than 60 per cent in domestic couple requests across the French, Swiss and Monegasque markets in three years. In France, couples account for 21 per cent of top staffing requests, largely because a principal who houses one couple obtains two full-time workers for the cost of one set of accommodation. The turning point came between 2018 and 2022, when international owners arrived in Switzerland, Monaco and Belgium in numbers and brought with them stricter confidentiality requirements, higher presentation standards and properties full of technology that somebody has to understand.

The job description has moved with the money. A couple is now responsible for general surveillance of the property, interior and exterior maintenance, technical equipment, liaison with service providers, supervision of works, access control and the reception of owners and their guests. On wine estates, historic châteaux and mountain chalets the seasonal rhythm adds a further layer, because the property has to be readied before anyone announces they are coming. Owners increasingly expect a near managerial approach: not simply executing tasks, but understanding, alerting, planning and reporting back. That upgrade in expectation explains a large share of the salary increase.

The shortage underneath all this is demographic. The majority of genuinely operational couples placed in 2026 are over 40, with long experience in demanding environments. Younger candidates are deterred by the requirement of permanent presence, by the isolation of many properties and by a long-term commitment that sits badly against a preference for mobility. Junior profiles are rare and need substantial support before they reach the autonomy a UHNW owner assumes. As the current cohort approaches retirement, the gap widens rather than closes.

One quieter change deserves attention from anyone entering the profession. Because accommodation is tied to the employment contract and justified by the necessity of on-site presence, owners in all four markets are now drafting far more carefully: what the accommodation includes, what it does not, what the occupants may do inside it, and how quickly it must be released if the relationship ends. Contractual clarity has become the standard response to a market in which both the property and the people are worth a great deal more than they were.
lead.why: The couple is the only household role hired as a single unit, which makes the private life of two people part of the employer's operating risk and part of theirs. Anyone entering estate work should read the accommodation clause with the same attention as the salary line.

articles.title: The wealthy stop choosing a country and start assembling a portfolio of them, and the United States scores 62.3
articles.body:
Henley & Partners published the 2026 edition of its Private Wealth Migration Report on 16 June, and it is the most substantial rewrite since the series began in 2023. Where earlier editions counted millionaires crossing borders, this one introduces a Global Wealth Mobility Framework built with the analytics firm AlphaGeo, scoring jurisdictions across 12 dimensions and 38 weighted indicators covering tax treatment, rule of law, quality of life, investor pathways, family inclusion, geopolitical stability and capital mobility. Findings are benchmarked against World Bank, IMF, OECD and Global Peace Index data and cross-checked against the firm's own enquiry and application flows.

The scores rearrange the familiar map. The United Arab Emirates records 85.3, among the highest in the framework. Singapore follows at 79.5 and New Zealand at 75.8, the latter after reforms to its Active Investor Plus visa. A second cluster includes the Cayman Islands at 74.3, Cyprus at 73.5, the Netherlands at 72.8, Portugal at 72.5 and Italy at 72.3, where a flat tax regime for new residents and a favourable inheritance framework have helped push Milan towards being a genuine family office centre. Switzerland sits at 70.8, Greece at 70.5 and Monaco at 70.0.

The jurisdictions classified as competitive but under pressure make less comfortable reading for anyone whose employer keeps a house there. Germany scores 69.7, Norway 69.0, the United Kingdom 68.3, South Korea 66.2 and France 65.7. Applications from individuals with a British address rose 15 per cent between 2024 and 2025, and so far in 2026 British citizens account for almost half of all applications processed from UK addresses, against 8 per cent in 2018. Enquiries from German nationals rose 16 per cent between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first of 2026, and France has climbed from the firm's top 40 source nationalities in 2024 to its top 15.

The United States is the paradox the report dwells on. It scores 62.3, well below its standing as the world's largest engine of wealth creation, and is simultaneously Henley's single largest source market. Applications from US nationals doubled in 2025 against the previous year and remain elevated. Only 7 per cent come from Americans living abroad, which means the demand is domestic. Nearly half of those applications are directed at European programmes and more than a quarter at Latin America and the Caribbean.

What is being bought is not relocation. In the first five months of 2026 the firm received applications from 86 nationalities across 47 investment migration programmes, and more than 28 per cent of applicants already lived outside their country of nationality. The pattern the report describes is a sovereign portfolio: residence in one jurisdiction, citizenship in another, business and banking structures in a third, so that no single government holds the whole of a family's life and capital. Even in the Emirates, where enquiries rose 41 per cent and applications for alternative residence 29 per cent between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first of 2026, the reading is diversification rather than exodus.
articles.why: The household follows the jurisdiction. A family holding residence in one country and citizenship in another needs staff who can be moved legally and quickly, which is why portability of a passport and a work permit is now a hiring criterion as real as references.

articles.title: Alpine prices rise for a fifth straight year, and the chalet stops being a winter house
articles.body:
Knight Frank's Alpine Property Report 2026 records a market moving against the grain. While a number of global prime residential markets slowed, prime ski homes rose 23 per cent on average over the past five years, and the firm's Alpine Property Index gained 3.3 per cent over the last twelve months.

The gains are concentrated rather than general. Andermatt leads the index at 14.6 per cent, a rise attributed in large part to the loosening of restrictions on foreign ownership there. Davos, the second most expensive resort on the index and a place that fills with heads of state once a year, rose 10.5 per cent. Cortina d'Ampezzo added 10 per cent. St Moritz and Méribel each rose 7.1 per cent, and Gstaad 6.2 per cent.

The reason given is not snow. Kate Everett-Allen, who heads European residential research at Knight Frank, describes Alpine property as having evolved from seasonal playgrounds into year-round sanctuaries. Flexible working, a durable interest in permanent mountain living and a continued appetite for wellness and open country have turned six-week houses into twelve-month ones. Resorts have responded by investing in schools, infrastructure and services that only matter if people are there in June.

The practical consequence is a different kind of house. A property occupied all year needs continuous maintenance, a supply chain that functions in the off season, and someone in place to run it when the family is not there. That is a materially different staffing problem from opening a chalet for a fortnight at Christmas and closing it again in April, and it is arriving in the same valleys where qualified live-in couples are already scarce.
articles.why: Year-round Alpine living converts the seasonal caretaker into a permanent household with a permanent payroll. For anyone building an estate career, the mountain resorts are becoming full-time postings rather than winter contracts.

articles.title: A charter is confirmed on WhatsApp at three in the morning, and the broker is not in the conversation
articles.body:
EnterJet, a London firm that says it handles around 900 charters a month through a broker-free online process, completed its first booking made entirely through WhatsApp this summer. The company's founder, Charles Robinson, now 25, who entered the industry at 17 and set up the business in 2024, spent a year building the AI agent behind it, named Celeste, on the reasoning that clients will use a messaging application already on their telephone but resent downloading and repeatedly logging into another one.

The details of that first booking are worth reading closely. The request was made at three in the morning and the flight cost USD 13,000, which Robinson claims would have been from 5 to 10 per cent more through a traditional broker, who in any case might not have been awake. The whole exchange took 46 minutes, of which 43 were the client considering options. Once the client accepted, confirmation took under 90 seconds and the flight briefing arrived as a PDF in the same thread. Celeste responds to an opening brief in from 30 to 45 seconds, and pricing and availability are drawn from operator feeds in real time rather than composed by the model. A human team supervises and takes over anything requiring judgement.

The trade is not uniformly convinced. Matt Feldon of the boutique broker Smart Aviation uses AI in the running of the business but doubts clients want it in the conversation, arguing that chartering an aircraft is a personal act and that a model has no empathy. His firm keeps someone on call around the clock and confirms bookings in anything from 15 minutes to an hour, though he concedes that depends on an operator answering. James Farley, co-chief executive of Victor, put the objection more sharply: discretion is fundamental to private aviation, clients expect confidentiality around their travel, their preferences and their personal information, and any use of AI has to be controlled so that it never costs that trust. He notes that even clients who built AI companies themselves still value the human relationship.

The direction of travel is nonetheless clear. Elevate Jet, a US operator of thirty years' standing, launched its own agent, Ruby, earlier in 2026 inside an application that matches trip requests to aircraft with instant pricing. Robinson observes that nothing in the architecture prevents a client's own AI agent from negotiating with his, given an itinerary, an aircraft requirement and a budget, which would remove the human from both ends of the transaction. He says his firm is not doing that today, but calls it a reasonable place for this to go next.
articles.why: The value of whoever books the aircraft is shifting from finding the price to exercising judgement, holding confidences and knowing the unwritten preferences of the principal. Those are precisely the things an agent cannot read off an operator feed.

articles.title: Rotation becomes standard above sixty metres, and the senior interior crew a yacht wants are already committed elsewhere
articles.body:
The 2026 interior salary guide published by YPI CREW, the Antibes crew agency, sets out what the yacht side of private service now pays and, more usefully, what it now concedes. A purser on a yacht of from 60 to 80 metres earns from 7,000 to 8,500 euros a month on equal rotation, from 8,000 to 10,000 euros on 80 to 100 metres, and from 8,500 euros above 100 metres. A chief stewardess on a 30 to 40 metre yacht earns from 4,000 to 6,500 euros with 60 days of leave, rising to from 7,500 to 10,000 euros on equal rotation once the vessel passes 80 metres. A junior stewardess of under a year's experience earns from 3,000 to 3,500 euros at any size, with from 60 to 90 days of leave.

The structural fact behind those numbers is that rotational roles are now standard on yachts over 60 metres, and a significant share of experienced senior interior crew are locked into long-term rotational posts. They are, in the agency's blunt phrasing, simply not available. That closes one door and opens another: a capable stewardess with a few seasons behind her can now step into a chief stew or head of service appointment considerably earlier than she could have expected five years ago, provided the yacht is willing to develop her.

Recruitment at the entry level is a different story. Candidate volumes keep rising, driven partly by television and social media, and a large proportion of those candidates leave within their first season, unprepared for long hours, constant proximity to guests and colleagues and service standards that do not relax. Those arriving from hotels or cruise ships adapt faster and stay longer, which is why service sector experience has become the differentiator at the bottom of the ladder rather than certificates.

At the top of the ladder the agency makes an observation that applies equally on land. Across all seniority levels, communication, adaptability and discretion are rated as important as technical service skill, and many crew departures that present as wellbeing problems can be traced to gaps in management capability at head of department level. Leadership training for the newly promoted, proper reference checks and cultural alignment at the point of hire are described as the most effective levers for reducing turnover.

The last shift is in what an interior department contains. Demand keeps growing for spa therapists, nurses, hairdressers, beauticians, personal trainers and yoga and Pilates instructors across the larger fleet, with Reformer Pilates increasingly requested by owners and guests. A spa therapist with advanced training earns from 4,000 to 5,500 euros a month, a nurse from 4,000 to 5,000, and a laundry master above 100 metres from 4,000 to 5,000 on equal rotation. These are specialists who rotate roles frequently in order to keep their qualifications current, which makes professional development a retention tool rather than a benefit.
articles.why: A house and a yacht now compete for the same person, and land-based service experience travels well in that direction. The yacht's answer to burnout, which is leave written into the contract, is the benchmark against which private households are increasingly judged.

articles.title: Two casks from a distillery that no longer exists sell for GBP 4.25 million, and the buyer inherits the decisions still to be made
articles.body:
On 10 March 2026 at Christie's in London, two casks from the original Karuizawa distillery in Japan sold for a combined GBP 4,250,000, around USD 5.65 million. Each cask made GBP 2,125,000 including buyer's premium, and together they became the highest value lots ever sold by Christie's Wine and Spirits.

The provenance explains the price. The casks, numbered 6195 and 888, were distilled in 1999, the final year before the original Karuizawa distillery ceased production, and no more will be made. They were offered from the private collection of Sukhinder Singh of Elixir Distillers, one of the most closely watched names in rare spirits, and had been maturing in a Speyside warehouse.

What distinguishes a cask from a bottle is that it is unfinished. Each of these yields roughly 420 bottles, and the buyer now holds influence over how the whisky matures from here, when it is bottled and how it is eventually released. That is a set of decisions rather than an object, and decisions of that kind require storage, insurance, monitoring and, at some point, action.

The wider spirits market gives the result its edge. The category-wide expansion of the last decade has given way to a more selective market in which volumes are softer and collectors fewer, but in which rarity, strong age statements and unrepeatable provenance still command serious money. A distillery that closed a quarter of a century ago is, by definition, the one thing the market cannot make more of.
articles.why: Collections of this kind arrive in the household as administration, not as shopping. Knowing that a cask carries a maturation decision, a bonded warehouse and an insurance line is part of the cultural fluency the job now assumes.

briefs.t: One in ten, and hard to fill
briefs.b: In the United States, estate managers account for 10 per cent of all household staffing requests, yet very few candidates combine the technical, security and management experience the role now demands. Estate managers routinely run large teams and work alongside protection staff, a level of responsibility that rules out most applicants.

The United States and the United Arab Emirates are now the fiercest and best-paying markets for private staff, with UAE compensation expected to reach from USD 120,000 to USD 140,000 as demand grows. In the United Kingdom, restricted access to EU workers since Brexit has tightened the London pool and pushed salaries upwards.

The United Kingdom carries the highest demand for nannies of any market, close to a quarter of all placements worldwide. Nanny placements run at a 96 per cent success rate and successful candidates typically arrive with six years of experience, with first aid training treated as standard rather than a distinction.

Greece has emerged as one of the clearest beneficiaries of Europe's shifting investment migration landscape, scoring 70.5 on Henley's new competitiveness framework after Spain closed its golden visa and Portugal withdrew its real estate linked route. The lesson drawn is that when governments close established pathways, demand does not disappear, it relocates.
